title: Number Systems — Rational and Irrational Foundations
subject: Mathematics
scope_summary: Canonical Grade 9 Mathematics Number Systems package for the first ten independently validated NCERT Exemplar Unit 1 questions: number-set inclusion and density, rational/irrational decimal characterisation, irrational examples and products, interval selection, recurring decimals, and addition of like surds. Atlas/rung enrichment is intentionally deferred.

resources.title: NCERT Exemplar Problems-Solutions Mathematics Class IX — Unit 1 Number Systems
resources.section: Unit 1: Number Systems · Exercise 1.1 Q1-Q10 and official answers
resources.rights_status: Official NCERT curricular source; repository stores source-bound question text, answer locators and validation evidence.
supports_claims: Every rational number is real, and rational numbers are dense in the real line.
Rational decimals terminate or recur; irrational decimals are non-terminating and non-recurring.
Irrational products can be rational or irrational depending on the factors.
Like surds combine by adding their rational coefficients.
resources.selection_reason: Direct official NCERT source for the ten Number Systems questions independently validated in Issue #211 / PR #212.

buckets.title: Number Systems Foundations
buckets.badge_reason: The questions are foundational but require precise distinctions among rational, irrational and real-number representations.

scope.covers: Grade 9 Number Systems concepts directly exercised by NCERT Exemplar Unit 1 Exercise 1.1 Q1-Q10.
excluded: Formal proofs of irrationality beyond elementary examples.
Exponent laws and rationalisation beyond the source questions.
Atlas/rung enrichment and advanced olympiad number theory.

capabilities.action: Classify elementary numbers within rational, irrational and real-number sets.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses definitions and exact simplification to distinguish rational from irrational examples and places rational numbers inside the real numbers.

capabilities.action: Use density and numerical bounds to identify rational numbers between real numbers.
capabilities.success_criterion: Shows that rational numbers are dense and verifies an explicit rational candidate lies inside a stated interval.

capabilities.action: Classify real numbers from terminating, recurring or non-recurring decimal behaviour.
capabilities.success_criterion: Connects terminating or recurring decimals with rational numbers and non-terminating non-recurring decimals with irrational numbers.

capabilities.action: Determine whether products of irrational numbers are necessarily rational or irrational.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses exact counterexamples to show that irrational×irrational may be rational or irrational.

capabilities.action: Combine like surds by operating on their rational coefficients.
capabilities.success_criterion: Recognizes a common radical factor and adds or subtracts its coefficients without multiplying the radical.

microtopics.title: Rational, Irrational and Real Classification
entry_assumptions: Can simplify elementary square roots and fractions exactly.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Move from the surface form of a number to the exact definition that determines whether it is rational, irrational and therefore real.

teaching_path.action: State the relevant set definition before classifying the number.
teaching_path.why_valid: Classification must be anchored to the definition of rational or irrational rather than appearance.

teaching_path.action: Simplify the number exactly where possible.
teaching_path.why_valid: An exact simplification can reveal an integer or rational quotient hidden by radicals or fractions.

teaching_path.action: Check the simplified form against the set definition and inclusion relation.
teaching_path.why_valid: A rational number is real; a non-square integer has an irrational principal square root.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every expression containing a radical is irrational.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does the radical simplify to a rational number, as √81 or √(4/9) does?
misconceptions.repair: Simplify first; then classify the exact result.

exit_task.prompt: Why is √81 rational even though it is written with a radical sign?

answer.summary: Because √81=9, and 9 is an integer and therefore rational.
reasoning: Evaluate the principal square root exactly: √81=9.
Every integer is rational because it can be written over denominator 1.
answer.check: The simplified value 9 belongs to the integers and rationals.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit result follows by exact simplification of √81 to the integer 9 and set inclusion.

microtopics.research_contribution: Provides the foundational rational, irrational and real classification mapping needed by the validated NCERT Exemplar Unit 1 admission subset.

microtopics.title: Rational Density and Interval Selection
entry_assumptions: Can compare positive real numbers and form the average of rational numbers.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Use either a constructive midpoint argument or exact numerical bounds to prove a rational lies strictly between two real endpoints.

teaching_path.action: Use density: between distinct rational numbers, their rational midpoint lies strictly between them.
teaching_path.why_valid: The midpoint (a+b)/2 is rational whenever a and b are rational and a<b.

teaching_path.action: Repeat the construction or compare a proposed rational with decimal bounds for irrational endpoints.
teaching_path.why_valid: Repeated midpoints give infinitely many rationals; decimal or squared bounds can verify an interval candidate.

teaching_path.action: Check both strict inequalities and rationality of the candidate.
teaching_path.why_valid: Being between the endpoints requires both inequalities, not just closeness to one endpoint.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: There is only one rational number between two rationals, or a decimal-looking candidate need not be checked against both endpoints.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: After finding one midpoint, can you find another midpoint between the left endpoint and that midpoint?
misconceptions.repair: Use repeated midpoint construction, and verify both interval inequalities for a concrete candidate.

exit_task.prompt: Give a rational number strictly between 1 and 2 and explain why there are infinitely many such rationals.

answer.summary: 3/2 is one example; repeated rational midpoints produce infinitely many more.
reasoning: (1+2)/2=3/2 is rational and lies between 1 and 2.
Taking further midpoints between rational endpoints keeps producing new rational numbers.
answer.check: Each midpoint is rational and strictly interior to its chosen rational interval.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit claim is established constructively by rational midpoint arithmetic.

microtopics.research_contribution: Provides the foundational rational density and interval selection mapping needed by the validated NCERT Exemplar Unit 1 admission subset.

microtopics.title: Decimal Character of Rational and Irrational Numbers
entry_assumptions: Knows place-value notation and the meaning of a repeating decimal.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Read termination or recurrence as a structural property of the represented real number rather than as a visual length of the decimal string.

teaching_path.action: Fix the criterion: a rational decimal terminates or eventually repeats; a non-terminating non-repeating decimal is irrational.
teaching_path.why_valid: This decimal-characterisation is equivalent to rational representability by a ratio of integers.

teaching_path.action: For a recurring decimal, use place-value algebra when an exact rational value is needed.
teaching_path.why_valid: Multiplying by a power of ten and subtracting cancels the repeating tail.

teaching_path.action: Distinguish a finite truncation from the infinite recurring decimal it approximates.
teaching_path.why_valid: A finite decimal such as 1.41421 is not equal to √2; recurring notation represents the infinite repetition.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any non-terminating decimal is irrational, or a displayed finite approximation equals the irrational number.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does the decimal eventually repeat a fixed block, or does its pattern fail to recur?
misconceptions.repair: Separate terminating, recurring and non-recurring infinite decimals before classifying.

answer.summary: Because it is recurring and equals 1/3 exactly.
reasoning: Thus x=1/3, a ratio of integers.
answer.check: 1/3 has decimal expansion 0.333..., confirming the exact equality.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit result is verified algebraically by converting the recurring decimal 0.333... to 1/3.

microtopics.research_contribution: Provides the foundational decimal character of rational and irrational numbers mapping needed by the validated NCERT Exemplar Unit 1 admission subset.

microtopics.title: Products of Irrational Numbers
entry_assumptions: Can multiply square roots and identify elementary irrational square roots.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Reject an 'always' claim by producing exact counterexamples with irrational factors whose products land in different number sets.

teaching_path.action: Treat 'always rational' and 'always irrational' as universal claims that one counterexample can refute.
teaching_path.why_valid: Universal statements fail when a valid case contradicts them.

teaching_path.action: Use √2·√2=2 and √2·√3=√6 as contrasting exact products.
teaching_path.why_valid: The first product is rational while the second is irrational.
teaching_path.output: one rational and one irrational product

teaching_path.action: Check that every factor used in both examples is itself irrational.
teaching_path.why_valid: √2 and √3 are irrational because 2 and 3 are not perfect squares.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The product of two irrational numbers must stay irrational.
misconceptions.repair: Use exact products to test universal claims instead of extrapolating from one example.

exit_task.prompt: Give one pair of irrational numbers whose product is rational.

reasoning: √2 is irrational.
√2·√2=2, which is rational.
answer.check: Both factors are irrational while the exact product is the integer 2.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit result uses the exact identity √2·√2=2 with irrational factors and rational product.

microtopics.research_contribution: Provides the foundational products of irrational numbers mapping needed by the validated NCERT Exemplar Unit 1 admission subset.

microtopics.title: Addition of Like Surds
entry_assumptions: Can factor a common algebraic factor from a sum.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Recognize a common radical as a factor and operate only on its rational coefficients.

teaching_path.action: Treat the shared radical as a common factor.
teaching_path.why_valid: Like surds have the same radical part, so distributivity applies to their coefficients.

teaching_path.action: Factor the radical and add the rational coefficients.
Expand the combined expression to recover the original two terms.
teaching_path.why_valid: Distribution reverses the factorisation and checks the coefficient arithmetic.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Adding √3+2√3 means multiplying the radicals or changing √3 into √6.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What common factor appears in both terms 2√3 and √3?
misconceptions.repair: Factor √3 first and add only the coefficients 2 and 1.

reasoning: Factor the common radical √5.
The coefficients give 4-1=3, so the result is 3√5.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit result follows from distributivity with the common factor √5.

microtopics.research_contribution: Provides the foundational addition of like surds mapping needed by the validated NCERT Exemplar Unit 1 admission subset.

question_families.title: Number-set classification from exact form

demand_dimensions.novelty: exact number-set classification after elementary simplification

safe_variations: Vary integers, rational fractions, and elementary square roots while keeping classification decidable by exact simplification.
transfer_boundaries: Does not extend to formal irrationality proofs or abstract set-theoretic constructions.
common_wrong_routes: Assuming any radical expression is irrational without simplifying.

question_families.title: Rational density and interval questions
solution_structure: Use density or bound the endpoints
safe_variations: Vary rational endpoints or simple irrational bounds while retaining a rational midpoint or directly checkable interior candidate.
transfer_boundaries: Does not cover completeness proofs, Dedekind cuts, or advanced density arguments.
common_wrong_routes: Treating one found rational as the only possible one; checking only one inequality.

question_families.title: Decimal representation and rationality
solution_structure: Apply the rational-decimal criterion or recurring-decimal algebra
Verify exact rather than truncated equality
safe_variations: Vary terminating, recurring, and visibly non-recurring decimal patterns while preserving an exact classification route.
transfer_boundaries: Does not cover base-dependent expansions or advanced proofs about normal numbers.
common_wrong_routes: Calling every non-terminating decimal irrational; treating a finite approximation as exact.

question_families.title: Irrational product counterexamples

demand_dimensions.novelty: counterexample-based closure reasoning for irrational products

safe_variations: Vary elementary irrational square roots so one product simplifies rationally and another remains irrational.
transfer_boundaries: Does not claim a general field structure for irrational numbers or advanced algebraic-number theory.
common_wrong_routes: Assuming closure of irrational numbers under multiplication.

question_families.title: Like-surd coefficient operations

demand_dimensions.novelty: coefficient combination for a common radical factor

safe_variations: Vary rational coefficients and the shared square-root factor while keeping the surds like.
transfer_boundaries: Does not cover unlike-surd simplification, rationalisation, or nested radicals.
common_wrong_routes: Changing the radical when adding like surds.

options: (B) there is exactly one rational number
(C) there are infinitely many rational numbers
(D) there are only rational numbers and no irrational numbers

answer.summary: (C) there are infinitely many rational numbers
reasoning: Use the rational midpoint (a+b)/2 between any rationals a<b. one interior rational.
Repeat the midpoint construction inside the smaller rational interval. arbitrarily many interior rationals.
Conclude that no finite list exhausts the rationals between the endpoints. infinitely many rationals.

reasoning_route.action: Repeat the midpoint construction inside the smaller rational interval.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Each repetition produces another distinct rational strictly between the original endpoints.

reasoning_route.action: Conclude that no finite list exhausts the rationals between the endpoints.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The construction can be repeated indefinitely.

answer.check: Repeated rational midpoints prove there are infinitely many rational numbers between two distinct rationals.
